Discipline to be key
We say it a lot when we talk about the Wallabies.
But those same conversations about discipline are happening in the halls of Twickenham as well as England comes off a horrific Six Nations campaign heading into this set of fixtures.
During the Six Nations, England received eight yellow cards and one red across five matches.
In total that equates to 118 minutes - almost a game and a half of rugby - without 15 men on the pitch.
That continued in July, when England finished the 45-21 defeat by South Africa with 13 men, and had four second-half sin-binnings against Argentina as they almost threw away a winning position.

"It has been a big internal discussion," Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney told the BBC. "Steve [Borthwick]'s very conscious of that and he's working really hard with the players to improve that aspect. "You need all your players on the pitch for as long as possible. That's something we need to address."
"It has been a big internal discussion," Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney told the BBC.
"Steve [Borthwick]'s very conscious of that and he's working really hard with the players to improve that aspect.
"You need all your players on the pitch for as long as possible. That's something we need to address."
Incredibly, England have only played one game in 2026 where they've kept 15 men on the field for the full game.
The Wallabies too have been criticised for their ill-discipline.
In the Wallabies' 10 internationals this calendar year they have been shown nine yellow cards and a red.
You'd have to think that if one of these teams keeps 15 men on the field for the full 80, they'll go a long way to securing victory.
Time for the national anthems
There's certainly a handful or more Australians in the crowd, with Advance Australia Fair getting a more than respectable airing in accompaniment to Emilia Bertolini.
The scale of the opposition is truly laid bare though soon after, with a raucous rendition of God Save The King, which echoes around the stadium.
Last Post and a moment's silence
A packed stadium falls silent as the Last Post is played, followed by a minute's silence.

And he's then followed by both teams together.
Remembrance Sunday
It is Remembrance Sunday in Great Britain, and there will be a minute's silence before kick off today - as there is in all sporting events across the nation.
Earlier on today, World Rugby chairman Brett Robinson and the chief executive of Rugby Australia, Phil Waugh, laid a wreath outside the Rose and Poppy Gates at Twickenham.
England vs Wallabies: Match preview
Wallabies have learned painful All Black lessons
The Wallabies say they have thoroughly reviewed last month's mauling by the All Blacks as they head into a month of Nations Championship tests in Britain.
Loosehead prop Angus Bell said the Wallabies had looked to address the weaknesses exposed by New Zealand in their 50-19 win in Auckland and then a runaway 43-21 triumph in Sydney a week later.

"Look, rugby is not really a linear line. There's a lot of ups and downs. Both in people's careers and with teams," Bell told a press conference on Wednesday. "As we know, it's always like a bit of a roller coaster, but as long as you're trending upwards, I think that's the main point of getting better collectively as a team and also individually."
"Look, rugby is not really a linear line. There's a lot of ups and downs. Both in people's careers and with teams," Bell told a press conference on Wednesday.
"As we know, it's always like a bit of a roller coaster, but as long as you're trending upwards, I think that's the main point of getting better collectively as a team and also individually."
Bell said the All Blacks had put Australia under pressure with the pace of their game.
"They were excellent at that, and that's where we struggled, and that's something that we've implemented in our training to get better.

"We didn't learn the lessons from the first test match, and then they exposed us on the other ones in the second and I feel like the training week we had prior to coming over here and also now today has been really good, and we've actually addressed those and fixed those."

The 26-year-old Bell said there had been many positives for the Wallabies in recent months under new coach Les Kiss as they put together an unbeaten run of six matches before the blowout against New Zealand.

"I guess my point is we've got to be able to change and manoeuvre between teams. Like England aren't going to be the same as the All Blacks. Do they suit us more or not? "It's all about how we prepare, how we train, how we play. We did cop a lot of criticism (after defeat by the All Blacks), but again, that's part of rugby and we know that it is."

Itoje fired up after horror 2026 for England

Maro Itoje sees victory over Australia as more than just a step forward in the new Nations Championship, with the England captain believing it's a golden opportunity to strike a major psychological blow ahead of next year's World Cup.
The old rivals will be meeting for the last time before the 2027 World Cup, with projections showing they could meet in a quarterfinal in Sydney on October 31 next year.
"Each game is new but there's no doubt that against teams you're going to play down the line, you want them to know that you've got their number," said Itoje yesterday.
"We want to win this weekend for this weekend's sake, but we also want to win because we don't want to give the opposition an inch.

"These are the games that get your blood pumping and you realise it's big. In terms of where we want to go and doing well in this competition, we want to respond to the inconsistencies of the Six Nations.
"We want to show ourselves and show England fans that we've turned a corner. For that reason, this game is huge."
England have had a pretty disappointing 2026 campaign, losing five of their eight Tests.
That included a dire 6 Nations campaign in which the English won just a single game against the hapless Welsh, while losing to Italy for the first time in their history.

"I have full confidence that the public, England fans and our families and friends in the stands are going to see a team that's fighting for one another, putting their best foot forward, that's aggressive and taking the game to Australia," Itoje said. "We want to set the tone of how this autumn is going to go and show the public what this team is about."

Mutinous England hit back at claims Steve Borthwick is under pressure
Today's clash is a vitally important one for both teams, but perhaps more so for England coach Steve Borthwick.
The former Bath and Saracens lock has been at the centre of reports that his management style prompted squad unrest and caused a toxic environment during the July tour.
England played South Africa at Ellis Park in Johannesburg, Fiji in Liverpool and then Argentina in Santiago del Estero in consecutive weekends throughout July, winning the latter two matches.
A report in the Times said unhappy players wanted summit talks with Borthwick and Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney in Argentina.
The players in the team have hit back at those reports.
"I can tell you that a lot of it's untrue," Jamie George told the BBC.
"We, as a squad, are incredibly disappointed by it.
"You just have to look at the timing of the article — two days out from our first Test match. I think it's clearly there to try and be divisive.
"Whoever's written this article, obviously their aim was for it to be divisive. Unfortunately for them, it's going to go the other way.

"This is going to galvanise us, it's going to make us tighter. We speak a lot about standing up for people, we speak a lot about helping each other, and we've got to make sure that we do that for Steve.
"He has had a bit of a personal attack here and an unwarranted one at that."
George's sentiments were echoed by skipper Maro Itoje yesterday.

"I can wholeheartedly say that Steve has not lost the faith of us players," Itoje said. "We back him 100 per cent. "We want to play for Steve, we want to represent him in a way that is fitting of the quality of coach he is. We're going to have to use everything to make sure we do the job."

"We back him 100 per cent.
"We want to play for Steve, we want to represent him in a way that is fitting of the quality of coach he is. We're going to have to use everything to make sure we do the job."
Twickenham is ready
No place for Beale in spring opener, but he still eyes home World Cup
There would have been few people who would have picked Kurtley Beale's name out of the hat for this spring tour.
But the 37-year-old answered the SOS call to join the squad, five years after his last appearance.
The veteran playmaker won the last of his 95 caps against Wales in 2021 but joined Les Kiss' squad in Britain.
Beale was also called up in Joe Schmidt's first Wallabies squad in 2024 but a serious Achilles injury denied him a comeback.
But now, after impressive form for the Force in Perth, Beale said the prospect of featuring at next year's World Cup had helped sustain his determination through the rough patches.
"Yeah, absolutely. It's always been a motivation of mine," he told reporters ahead of Australia's clash with England at Twickenham on Sunday.
"But I've really just kind of focused on the now and not thinking too far ahead of myself and making sure that I'm at my best here for the team.
"I always thought I was able to still add to the group, to the game. And I just kept believing. I felt like there was some unfinished business."
Incredibly, despite his country coming calling, the Force aren't convinced he can play an entire Super Rugby season next year.
He has only managed to secure a 'train and trial' deal for next season and is unsure whether he will be elevated to the main squad.
"I don't know. I just know that I'm there to be able to train and play next year," he said.
Beale was not included in today's match day squad, but with two more tests against Scotland and Wales to come, there may well be further opportunities.

'Hero-worshipped' by Boks and All Blacks in Japan, Mark Nawaqantiawase finding his feet in union
Former Wallaby Berrick Barnes has revealed how even Springboks and All Blacks greats "hero-worshipped" Mark Nawaqanitawase upon his arrival in Japan.

Fresh off becoming the only player to capture this year's NRL premiership after completing an Ashes and State of Origin series-winning double, Nawaqanitawase has begun the latest chapter of an already-decorated career at the Saitama Wild Knights.
Barnes is the backs and attack coach under the club's director of rugby, former Wallabies mentor Robbie Deans, and couldn't be happier to have the freakish code-hopper on board.
"We're so lucky to have him. Forget the player, there's an aura and energy about him which is rare. He's a rare human being," Barnes told AAP from just outside Tokyo.
"He's just really positive around the group and lifts the Japanese boys up. He only lobbed on Thursday and already knew a lot of the boys' names.
"He'd even watched some footage and was over how we played. Not many guys come in and do that. Like, you'd think that's the bare minimum, mate, but that's pretty rare."
Barnes, a one-time Wallabies vice-captain after starting in the NRL as a teenage wonder at the Brisbane Broncos, has played with and under an endless list of legends of both codes.
Yet he was still blown away by the way Nawaqanitawase was feted by teammates and Wild Knights staff, including two-time Rugby World Cup winners Damian de Allende and Sam Whitelock.
"The aura he's got, he walks into a building and he even gives you belief as a coach, which is pretty rare from a player," Barnes said.

"I'm just excited for him to be around the boys. They're a great bunch we've got here and they'll welcome him in, but I've never seen a bunch of foreigners in our team actually genuinely excited to see someone in the building — and genuinely nervous.

"The Kiwi boys included. They deal with some pretty famous Kiwi guys — All Blacks or whatever — but Mark's status in what he's done in rugby league, it's ridiculous and, for a lot of those boys, there's a bit of hero worship there.
"We've got Damian de Allende, Lood de Jager, two players probably most considered like Mark in South Africa. We have Sam Whitelock, who came up and coached.

"So guys who've done a lot in the game, but I'd say there's not many that have had that 'Marky Mark' presence with guys. It's like 'holy shit, this guy's that good and we get to have him on our team'. That's pretty bloody cool."
Barnes believes the dual international will revel in Japan — and become an even superior player without the spotlight, glare and pressures from NRL or Australia's Super Rugby Pacific fans.
"Honestly, he'll get around with anonymity, seriously," Barnes said.
"That's what people don't get about Japan. It is an island unto itself. It's culturally unique.
"Yeah, on game day for sure he'll get mobbed by fans. The rugby fan base here is strong and they're passionate. But outside of games, he'll get around as if he's just an everyday bloke.

"After a while fans will recognise him, but people have to understand no-one watches rugby league over here. It's a weird thing because in Australia it's on everything and it's our main sport, especially on the east coast.
"But over here, mate, no one even knows who Nathan Cleary is."

Live rugby union: England vs Wallabies
Hello everyone and welcome to a very late night showing of rugby union action from London.
My name is Simon Smale and I am prying open my bleary eyes at this shocking hour to bring you all the action as it happens over there at the stately home of English rugby in the capital's south west.
It's time for the spring tour, and a clash against an England team that were absolutely horrid during the Six Nations, winning just one game against the even-worse Welsh.
The Wallabies are hardly in sparkling form themselves, losing their last two against New Zealand.
But that All Blacks blind spot aside, the Wallabies were on a six-game unbeaten run before getting bashed in the Bledisloe.
Will we see a return to the sort of form that saw Les Kis's team beat the Springboks in Perth?
Or will it be a similar story to last year when England ran out 25-7 winners at Twickenham?
Only time will tell, so let's head to Twickers to see what we can find out.
